Under RD-2's non-metered branch, detour mileage does not enter a fixed fare (any rebate would be limited to ERP/tolls or unpublished post-trip add-ons), so even if the single off-route segment counts, the recoverable amount is zero [F4][F6][RD-2]. The rate arithmetic is not applicable here: distance fare $19.67 ÷ 13.95 km = $1.4100/km, but the 4.08 km of extra driving [F3] was never billed, so 4.08 km × $1.4100/km = $5.75 is not a charge the rider paid and cannot be refunded on a fixed-quote trip [F3][F6][RD-2].

One off-route segment exists: 22:33–22:42, 5.74 km driven where the optimal route covers 1.66 km, +4.08 km and up to 1450 m off route, on a trip that ran 18.5 km against a 14.0 km optimal route (+33%) [F1][F3], so the RD-1 shortest-and-most-direct duty is engaged [RD-1].

The driver's traffic justification cannot independently exempt that segment: the only speed-band fact is Central Expressway band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 22:06–22:33 [F11], and band evidence is corroborative only under RD-4(b) (a single band does not exempt), while no traffic incident near the route is recorded [F14], so RD-4(a) fails and the segment falls through to RD-2 [F11][F14][RD-4].

The decisive question is the scope of the rider's consent. The driver asked at 22:29 "Jam on Central Expressway is building up ahead, can I go round via Lower Delta Road?" [F7] and the rider answered at 22:29 "Sure, go ahead." [F8]; the chat record is complete and every message timestamped [F9], so the rider's own message precedes the 22:33 segment start [F3][F8][RD-5].
